sentences.text: The dream island of Tenneref.
Millions of tourists come here for the sunshine, sand, and the sea.
But for many locals,
life is a nightmare.
Rents are skyrocketing,
and there's a shortage of affordable housing.
More and more people are squatting in vacant buildings while owners are fighting to repossess their
homes.
The island is caught between a tourism boom and a housing crisis.
It's a conflict found all across Europe.
a Russian Orthodox church right in the middle of Tenneref.
A few years ago, Russian investors began building a whole complex here in the south of
the island, but the apartments were never completed.
The pandemic and then the war in Ukraine
caused the investors to abandon the project.
The church is closed.
The planned vacation apartments are mere ruins,
evidence of a failed investment.
But they're not empty.
That's because people here desperately need a roof over their head.
Many see these ruins as a good housing option.
We're on Tenneref,
one of the eight Canary Islands west of Africa that belong to Spain.
Attorney Jose Abbit Boy Matoss
was born and raised on Tenneref
and knows the island well.
He says entire hotels are being squatted nowadays
as he's about to show us.
He's never seen a housing crisis like this before. He says
Hotel Marino had to close 6 years ago because of the co pandemic.
>> When it closed, the lower floors were bricked up to prevent squatters from moving in.
But people broke through the walls, climbed inside,
trashed parts of the building, and occupied the apartments.
>> Once squatters have moved into an empty building, evicting them can take months or years due
to lengthy legal proceedings.
The squatters of this hotel by the sea don't want to talk to us.
We're not allowed to film either.
We have to leave.
I understand that some people really are desperate,
but as I see it,
the vast majority are exploiting loopholes in the system.
They know that if they stay in a property for more than 3 days without the
owner filing a complaint,
they can stay there.
When a building has been left vacant, police are generally not allowed to evict squatters immediately.
A court has to issue an eviction order first.
Another construction ruin occupied by people not paying rent.
There's no electricity, which is why the building has so many solar panels. There's no running
water either.
>> People here have solar panels and water tanks.
Rents are much too high.
If I could afford an apartment, I wouldn't be living here.
>> He's lived here for 10 years and has to get by on just €900
a month.
This woman moved in with her baby 3 weeks ago and doesn't want to show her
face.
>> We looked for a room for ages, but couldn't find anything.
Everything's very expensive, and landlords have a lot of requirements.
They're asking for €650
for one room, and they want a security deposit of 3 months rent in advance.
You also need an employment contract lasting at least 6 months.
That's more than she can afford.
Instead, she paid a one-time fee of €3,000
for her room.
She was told she can stay until she's evicted.
She doesn't want to tell us who she paid the money to.
For many, squatting is the only way to find a home.
But it's also become a shady business in its own right. According to Javier Cabrera,
chairman of the business association in southern Tenneref.
Squatting has become a business. Everyone here knows it. There are people who specifically seek out
empty apartments, fix them up, and illegally set up electricity.
They list the apartments and collect money from the people who move in.
It's like a real estate agency.
except that they're dealing in properties with absolutely no permission from the owners.
In other words, a black market for squatting in empty apartments
rented out at a lower price.
We get a call from entrepreneur Muhammad Debbar,
originally from Lebanon.
He's been living in Tenneref for decades.
He's heard that we were filming at the Hotel Marino
and says he owns some of the apartments there, which he bought just recently.
Now he says he's renting them out cheaply to help people.
He insists
residents there aren't squatters.
These are all people who work and live here with their families.
I rent the apartments to them for a fixed price of €500.
It's my way of helping.
But how much did you pay for the apartments?
I don't have to answer that question. A lot of money.
>> So, you're incurring a loss?
>> No, I'm not losing money.
Look, when you help people, it can make them much happier.
For me, it's humanitarian aid.
I'm making my own apartments available to people who urgently need them.
>> Muhammad Debbar is a well-known and controversial
businessman on the island.
We can't verify his claims.
He's founded a political party, Fuetsza
Canaria,
and plans to field a candidate in the next mayoral election.
He won't say who he bought the apartments from.
There's one thing everyone can agree on. Tenneref is in dire need of social housing,
but in over 4 years, builders have constructed none.
However, they are busy building 44 new hotels across the Canary Islands.
Tourism is the engine of the economy,
but for many, it's also a curse.
Many landlords are investing in apartments to rent them out online as vacation rentals.
These properties are more profitable and less risky.
But this trend is what is fueling the housing shortage and driving up prices.
On Tenneref, the average rent has more than doubled in the last 5 years.
Residents have long been protesting all over the Canary Islands and throughout Spain.
in Barcelona
and Madrid.
>> Were you aware of this that there's a housing problem around here? >> No, it's been
we know it's in Ireland anyway that there's a lot of housing
that's just
all over Europe
everywhere.
>> On the other hand though,
you can't just tell people what to do with their own apartments.
But I think there's going to have to be a political solution soon
with more social housing which has been neglected for so long
in Germany too.
Instead of social housing, there are pretty cafes to attract tourists.
There's a clear need for different policies,
but nothing is happening and no politician was willing to speak with us either.
Here in the island's capital, Santa Cruz de Tenneref,
people have been staging a camping protest in front of the government headquarters for several days
now.
Over 100 people have set up tents.
They are being supported by numerous social initiatives throughout Spain.
We all want to pay rent and live in an apartment, but prices keep going up
and it's created a lot of mistrust.
People affected view others as the enemy, but the real enemy might actually be the bank,
which will buy up their homes.
Then they'll be evicted, too.
A mistrust that small property owners in the Canary Islands know all too well.
Enrique Reyes bought two apartments 2 years ago as an investment.
He wanted to rent them out to tourists, but things turned out differently.
Squatters beat him to it.
>> One day out of the blue, they showed up, broke the lock, and just walked right
in.
They settled in and ordered a couple of pizzas or something like that,
just to have legal proof.
Yes. So they could say, "We're here."
And that was that.
I think >> he called the police. But when squatters move into an empty apartment,
the court usually has to rule on the eviction
and that can take years.
The squatters lived in his two apartments for 2 years, severely damaging the properties.
Enrique had to continue paying the mortgage, taxes,
and common area fees during those years.
>> This is my property.
How can someone get away with taking it over like that?
And you can't even kick the person out.
Eventually,
Enrique hired a private eviction company.
Their strategy was to put pressure on the squatters till they decided to leave.
These methods are controversial,
but the company's services are in high demand throughout the Canary Islands.
Enrique says he had to pay the squatters €6,000
to get them to leave.
The eviction company cost him another €12,000,
but he thinks it was worth it.
Squatters have taken over properties all over the island.
There's no electricity here either, and the water tanks on the roof have to be filled
by the residents themselves.
The house is dilapidated.
Many of the people who live here work in hotels.
Do you speak Spanish? Not much. Can we ask you a question?
>> They don't want to speak on camera.
This woman is from South America and works as a kitchen assistant in a hotel.
She says she doesn't earn enough and has to rely on the black market for housing.
On the other side of the road,
most people are home owners.
All the apartments over there, right behind ours, the entire block on both sides, they're all
squatted.
>> I understand that some people have no choice.
But others squat just because they want to. They even have jobs.
I work in the hotel industry myself.
I know what people earn there.
If both partners are working, it's enough to get by.
The question is what people choose to spend their money on.
I have a simple Chinese cell phone, but sure if you absolutely have to have an
iPhone 17 Ultra.
>> He doesn't dare leave his apartment for more than a week.
He's installed cameras and an alarm system to deter squatters.
A few weeks after filming, we see on social media that many of these squatted apartments
have been cleared
by the eviction company that Enrique had hired.
After renovating both apartments,
Enrique sold them. He says buying more property is out of the question.
The world, he says, has completely changed.
>> It used to be perfectly normal. You'd come back from military service, find a job, get
married, and buy a house. It's just the way it was. Because back then, there was
still a middle class.
Today, it's gone.
a vanishing middle class,
rising rents,
not enough affordable housing.
It's a problem that's not unique to Tenneref,
as people across Europe know all too well.
